utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll go into closed session to allow the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will proceed in the following order: General Pavkovic, General Lazarevic, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Milutinovic, General Ojdanic, and General Lukic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, good morning, Witness K90.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The cross-examination by counsel representing the various accused will now take place. You'll be asked questions by each one in turn. I remind you that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you gave at the beginning of your evidence continues to apply to that evidence today. Now, the first counsel to examine you this morning will be Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, with the usher's assistance, I have a couple of documents I would like to have him give to the witness -- have her give to the witness, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we'll be looking at those documents in a few moments. We don't need to look at them right now, but very soon we will. The first question I want to ask you is: When did you first have an opportunity to look at your written statement in the Serbian language? When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it seems that that was the troublesome moment as far as the statement I saw is concerned. The interpreter who took the statement together with the investigator in Belgrade is not the person who signed the statement. And the witness -- the witness statement was not made during the course of two days but only one day. I cannot be very specific, but I think that once I met the investigator near the Hotel M - and that's when they had that traffic accident in front of the hotel. Well, maybe it wasn't the same day - and then in a park in Belgrade. I'm not sure that they read the statement back to me then. The first lady who interpreted what I said is I think more -- that statement, rather, is more reliable than the one I got here. Actually, the Prosecutor did not immediately give me a statement, but it was given to me in my room so I could see it; then I prepared it with the Prosecutor, and I made my objections, not in terms of the content of the statement, but certain observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When was it given to you in your room? After you came here for your testimony in this case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, one of the papers that I've just given you is a paper called a supplemental information sheet. It's that stapled piece of paper, and that's in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you ever seen that before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just have a look at this. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this is Mr. Hannis's report about your conversations with him on Friday, and it contains the things that you thought should be changed in your statement and the new things that you said that were not in your statement. From your testimony yesterday about things you say you told Mr. Hannis, I take it that it's your position that this document is not correct, that it does not contain all the information that you gave Mr. Hannis on Friday. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I and Mr. Hannis looked at the statement on Friday, and we agreed on most things except that we spelled out certain things in more precise terms and then protective measures were supposed to be imposed as well. So there was no contest regarding the bulk of the statement but only certain details, to have them spelled out precisely in the statement. Yesterday, when the Presiding Judge instructed me to review my statement, I reviewed it several times, and in addition to that the subsequent statement given to me. And I have no objections except for a few things that are now in this version that I handed in. So there's not any major deviation, but anyway this is what we talked about on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me -- I'm sorry, Mr. Ackerman, but let me be clear about this. I should have dealt with it at the beginning. Is there any other alteration that you wish to make to this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I hand this statement over to you, Your Honour, the one that I corrected? There are very few corrections there, and small ones, too, and then you will say what you have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If the corrections are in the Serbian language, I will not be able to read them. Therefore --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I just want you to see the number of corrections, and then you will decide whether that -- well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, we need to deal with each one that's necessary. So you tell me from your statement which paragraphs you wish to make alterations to. Which is the earliest paragraph you wish to alter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to read the paragraphs one by one and I'll tell you exactly what it is that I altered, and then you will -- well, let's start. Paragraph 28. This is the Prosecutor's correction, the 549th Motorised Brigade, so that was that imprecision that -- all right. The next one. In paragraph 36, the second sentence: "For such an occasion, we always carried aerosol air freshener cans." That wasn't the case. I said in this situation we used et cetera, et cetera. So that's the only change case. Paragraph 39.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing there. It's just the separation -- well, there's no change here. There was this one man and -- well, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That was dealt with yesterday, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Paragraph 41. The Prosecutor added, in the first sentence, the following was inserted: "It was not my unit's primary task."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And another sentence which is very important for me and it changes the text or context of what was inserted later. My major never issued an order to expel villagers, or rather, that they be expelled to Albania. That is the sentence that was subsequently added by the Prosecutor. So that's one of the changes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you also gave a full explanation of that yesterday, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. Then paragraph 43. "With my unit, I was involved in the expulsion." That's what is written here, but I said "relocation," I did not say "expulsion." It is not the same word. And here it says "from a few villages." That's what the Prosecutor added; and then the word "expelled" should be replaced by "relocated." All the villagers, all the inhabitants of that village, and then it says here "to compel them." Well, I explained to you yesterday, Your Honours, I did not have any specific orders what I was supposed to do if somebody were tell me, I don't want to leave. I would probably inform my supreme commander and they would decide what was to be done, but I really did not know what I was supposed to do. I mean, we did not have such a case and we did not have any precise instructions as to what we should do if somebody were to refuse. Then 44, it says "expulsion." I want "relocation" again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 45, you and I yesterday -- well, you asked me about that theft, Your Honour. Nobody dared take anything from the houses; these people who came individually, I, another person, and yet another person, and so on. It doesn't matter whether it was one or three people. It is important that they were searching people's belongings and searching through their houses, but it wasn't all the troops that were doing that. It was just individuals, and that's what I wrote here. Have I explained this clearly to the Court what it was that I was trying to say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 46. As for paragraph 46, I said then and I'm saying now that that is my indirect knowledge from other people. I had to admit now that on Saturday I talked to a man about that incident that occurred in Korisa, and he confirmed to me that my statement is almost all right, except that these people were up on this hill and then they moved towards the village and towards Albania; and then they left them there at some warehouse and that's where they were hit. So the incident is similar, but this is my indirect knowledge. I was not a participant. It's not my direct knowledge. So that's what I added to this part here that I changed. Have you understood what it was I was trying to say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me try to understand it. Yes, I do understand. Yes, carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 47. It has to do with -- well, it says here in the last sentence: "Everyone wore the well-known Frenki hats." I consulted this man on Saturday and he told me what I thought, too. And this is also an imprecision and it was due to translation. It was the SAJ that wore hats like that or similar hats, the special operations unit and some people from the PJPs, policemen, ordinary policemen, not special units. So possibly it was my mistake that this man I saw there with yet another man was not a member of the JSO. So let's clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't understand that. You told us yesterday that these familiar Frenki hats were red berets.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, that's right. Frenki hats were worn -- well, not Frenki hats. These little hats were worn by the SAJ and special operations units, but I saw this man there with the hat; and then I thought that it was the special operations units, maybe that's a mistake. Maybe I made a mistake. Maybe somebody had a hat, but I did not see the entire unit there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, now I don't understand. Your statement says: "About 400 additional police arrived. They included PJP units and Frenki's." And then yesterday you said they also included a unit for special operations, and by that were you also -- are they the same unit? That's Frenki's unit, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that's an additional unit that was there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this man I saw with a mask on his face and with this little hat, I thought that they were there. You know why I said this? Because -- well, a member of my group is a man that they were looking for, so that he returned to his unit because he was a reservists of this special operations unit. And I thought that they were out there in the field because of that, and that is why I gave this correction now with the possibility that I made a mistake originally. But the fact remains that the man with the mask and with the little hat was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Witness, the statement says, "they all," "all," wore the familiar Frenki hats, not one person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I corrected it. I saw two men, not the whole unit. Two men, who was -- were there in a passenger car, and I exchanged cigarettes for fruit juice with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now you say it's two. And you also say in the statement --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes -- well, I refer to two people a moment ago. I referred to a man and then another man, so it's two men. At this place and the place where this happened, there were two policemen. And this is where I saw this man there, but I don't know that he wasn't from that unit. He wasn't from that unit for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your statement at the moment says: "I recognised the Frenki's by their uniform."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hats. Hats that were worn by the special operations unit and the mask that he had on his face. That's why I thought that they were somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, your statement proceeds on the basis that you saw this yourself, not on the basis that you asked somebody about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, who is the person you say you were speaking to on Saturday about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that somebody here or is it somebody you telephoned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was there -- who's here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who's here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. A man who had been there on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if we should go into private session to discuss this any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The court shouldn't be in this position, Mr. Hannis, of dealing with this way. This is just dreadful. When witnesses are to have some of their evidence presented in writing, the Prosecution should have it sorted out so that it's clear what the witness can swear to. And in this case, we are having to clarify all sorts of things. We may get to the stage where we think it's inappropriate to admit this statement. Where will you be then?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be where I am, but I have to defend myself, Your Honour. I went through this with him when we proofed him. I asked him if there were any additional corrections beyond the ones that he put in the supplemental investigation. I was not told that there were any others required. When he came to testify, he said there were some additional ones. I went through and he listed a couple of specific ones. I asked him then when he was testifying were there any others, and he said I don't think so, maybe we'll talk about them when we come to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is the old story of doing this at the last minute. This is inevitably what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, you will recall this is a witness who we subpoenaed and who refused to come. This is a witness that the day he arrived refused to come to my office for proofing when Victims and Witnesses went to pick him up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And tell me the next change you wish to make. Approximate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says,"There is a small group here and their task was to take care of the people," but I wanted it to say "KLA," not "people," not "civilians."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 52.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And tell me again what's the change that you wish to make?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Instead of the word "people" - I take "people" to mean "civilians" - I wanted it to say "KLA" instead of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the sixth line, Your Honour, where the word "people" appears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That doesn't make any sense to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it does. The remaining part of my unit was deployed along this road. In places that are marked as P on the diagram, there is a small creek there. And they were to ensure that people did not escape through there into Djakovica, and I wanted to say to ensure that the KLA did not escape through there to Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And read the rest of the sentence: "But rather stayed on the road." So the KLA were going to politely walk on the road, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. We're not understanding each other. Part of the unit was along the road, and another part was along that brook that I drew on that map yesterday, if you remember the crossroads and the brook there. And that was discussed, and where Letic was wounded, where part of the unit was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How was it you identified the KLA on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not establish that. We -- it just says here that we were deployed there, soldiers, to protect people from escaping. They were not there to protect people, or rather, to prevent them from escaping, but rather from letting the KLA get into Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the next change you wish to make?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It continues from there. When they were taking men out and when they were threatened by guns, they were taken to a complex of certain buildings marked as E. The policemen were also forcing the men to sing Serb nationalist songs as they were moving to the locality there. They only forced the last group to sing, not all of them. That's what I wrote in that other paragraph. So it was just the last group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The next change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where it says the policeman was very harsh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have the paragraph numbers in this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've been able to give them to us so far.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But now in this new statement there aren't any numbers. See, no numbers here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which page are we on now then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 10 here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Page 10. And counting from the top, which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last sentence before the beginning of paragraph 61.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The policeman was very rough, was very dismissive, and told me they were slaughtering Siptars." Your Honours, I clarified this. I never said "slaughtering Siptars."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You said "skinning Siptars," so we got that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not "skinning." I explained to you what I meant when I said that. That the word I used can, of course, mean skinning someone; but when I used the word, it could mean that they were "killing" them. It doesn't necessarily mean they took a knife and skinned them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Witness K90, this is just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] but it cannot be translated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is just a nonsubject to be arguing about. It's clear that the intention was to say that they were killing them. So let's move on. What's the next change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 61, it says from five to ten men, but as I explained yesterday there were only between eight and ten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've had that already. Tell me any new change you wish to make to this statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There aren't any more. There aren't any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, you said at the beginning of your evidence today that the interpreter who signed this was not the interpreter who was there when the statement was translated. And we have a certificate by that interpreter saying that she was the person who read it to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I gave the statement to the investigator, there was only the investigator, myself, and that woman, not the woman who signed the statement but another woman. And from time to time, a man came in who introduced himself, but I don't know what his name is, but he was with us only from time to time, not all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Someone read it over to you in your language. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember about it being read back to me on that day; but when I signed it, they probably did or maybe they didn't. Because as it is now I would certainly have corrected it. Had it been read to me, I would certainly have corrected it. I don't remember the statement having been read back to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you'll see that there's a certificate attached to it by the interpreter, Emina Vukic, who says that this was orally translated in your presence and you appeared to have heard and understood it, and that happened on the 8th of December. And your signature on the front page has underneath it the 8th of December in writing that looks like you may have written it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it took me one day to give the statement here; whereas, it says here that I made the statement over two days. I don't remember the exact date, but I know that I was in the office only once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is possible that you made the statement on one day, and on the following day it was read over to you and you signed it. Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. Not the next day, I'm sure, because the gentleman who took the statement went back to his country and then they came back again. It was the new year, and then we saw each other in January or February, I don't know exactly when, in front of Hotel M or in a park; if it was the same day in one of the parks in Belgrade, but certainly not in the Tribunal office in Belgrade. I was there only once, and it was then that the young lady who signed the statement was there. The first time it was another lady from Belgrade. I am certain about that. When the investigator was there and I gave the statement to him, there was another woman there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, can you help us on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point in time I can only go by what's in the written document. I will try and contact the people listed here to see what I can clear up for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not the most important element here because the statement has now been read again by the witness, he's made the necessary corrections. What's your motion in relation to that now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender his statement. I can make further corrections based on his comments this morning and submit that document to him and then to you, to give him a chance to confirm that I've made the changes he wanted this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, what's your position in relation to the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think what Mr. Hannis suggests is probably the appropriate way to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The problem is when are we going to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, during the break I can try to make some arrangements for somebody from my office to assist based on what's in the transcript this morning, and have the language assistant who worked on it yesterday make those additional corrections; and then immediately after he finishes here, have him review it. If he indicates he's satisfied, I'll advise the Court and Defence counsel and then tender that version once it's typed up and completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what we'll do is continue with the cross-examination, hold the question of admitting this statement in reserve. We'll complete the cross-examination. At that stage, it will then be over to you to deal with the statement in the way you suggest. The final version will have to be available before the cross-examination is concluded, so we're going to have to allow a completion of the cross-examination, just in case there's anything in it that requires to be further explored by counsel, and that means that the re-examination will also have to be held over until this exercise is complete. So let's see how far we can get with that. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I just make one point. Based upon what I've heard now, it appears that paragraph 46 is not anything that witness has any direct knowledge of, but he's testifying about what someone else knows. I think that that shouldn't be a part of the statement. I think it should be stricken from the record, if that is indeed the case. I mean, we can have that witness testify when he gets here, but we can't have a witness testify about what another witness knows that he doesn't know.. I mean, that defeats the purpose of having a sworn statement based upon the affiant's knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that that is the case because the alternative is open to the Prosecutor to ask him questions about what he's heard about these events, so it comes to the same thing. And having it in writing in advance of course gives you, normally, a better notice of what's to be said. But that's a matter we'll take up when it comes to deciding finally whether to admit the statement and whether any parts of it should not be admitted. You must proceed on the basis, though, that this in some form will be part of his evidence. Because if it's struck out as a result of successful cross-examination, then no doubt it could come back in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, on Friday when you met with Mr. Hannis, can you tell us about how long it was that you actually spent with him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a lot. We clarified my objections to the statement very quickly. He noted it down, and that was the end of it. He didn't ask me to do anything inappropriate. He didn't try to persuade me to do anything. I just told him what my comments were, he put the questions he had to put about that, and that was it. I can't remember exactly how long it took, perhaps about an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you think your total time with Mr. Hannis on Friday was about an hour? Or was it longer than that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was more than an hour, but I can't tell you exactly how long it was. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't remember when you started and when you ended that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I take it you do not speak English?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And as far as you know, Mr. Hannis does not speak Serbian?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So that your conversation with Mr. Hannis was through an interpreter; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you have no idea what the interpreter told Mr. Hannis you were saying; you just know what you were saying in your own language. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when the young lady who was interpreting told Mr. Hannis what I had said, she told me what he said. I don't think she said anything that would change the context of the statement. When Mr. Hannis asked me a question -- please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions about your testimony yesterday in that regard. At page 8 of yesterday's transcript, Mr. Hannis was asking you some questions about corrections to your statement. And it had something to do with relocation of people. And you told us at that time that that was one of the things that you discussed with him on Friday. And, of course, you recall that as you were giving that testimony you were under oath. You had sworn to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and is it true then that on Friday you did have discussions with Mr. Hannis about this issue of expulsion versus relocation and so forth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told Mr. Hannis that what it said in the statement, as I also said today, should be "relocation" rather than "expulsion." I clearly let it be known that it referred to relocation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. And then you were asked about --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm not sure whether we discussed it at all. I can't remember exactly what we discussed, but I do know that this should be relocation. It was never my intention to say "expulsion." If we did discuss this, I certainly said it was "relocation."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were then asked if you had any other changes you wanted to make regarding this issue of relocation or expulsion. And at page 10 of your testimony yesterday, you said to Mr. Hannis: "On Friday I said to you, and today I'm going to say to this honourable Trial Chamber, that what is written here is not quite precise; that is to say, that my major never ordered the expulsion of villagers, that is to say to have them expelled to Albania. The order was always that these people should be directed towards Djakovica and the first villages here Djakovica." Now, is it true that you told Mr. Hannis that on Friday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that, and Mr. Hannis put it in the new statement that I received yesterday. He put in that correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. And then right after that, you said: "The population was not relocated until the cluster bombs started falling." Did you tell Mr. Hannis that on Friday, or is that something you told us for the first time yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I told Mr. Hannis that on Friday, yes, and in paragraph 42 that's what it says here in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then in -- on pages [sic] 34 and 35 of your statement, you talk about the relocation of people from the village Zub, where I think there was a VJ command post. You say that: "Not at any moment did we say to them that they should leave the state or the country. Why would they stay out there on their own at the mercy of aircraft?" And then you said to Mr. Hannis: "I explained it to you on Friday when I said on their own, that is what I meant when I was speaking a few minutes ago, to say that other soldiers did not take part. I told you on Friday and I'm telling the honourable Judges now. I don't know how we would have reacted if somebody said they had protested and didn't want to leave. I don't know. Perhaps the commander would have to come and tell them we didn't have any orders like that." You've made that correction now about three times in your testimony. My question is: Did you tell that to Mr. Hannis on Friday, as you said in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I have an objection to the question, because it's not clear to me whether Mr. Ackerman's question is about did he tell Mr. Hannis that other soldiers did not take part on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Because if that's what it is, I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I'm referring to, about halfway down page 35, where he says to you, Mr. Hannis: "I told you on Friday that I'm telling the honourable Judges now. I don't know how we would have reacted if somebody had protested and said they didn't want to leave. I don't know."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my problem is I see on the transcript, it says: "I don't know how we would have reacted," and the sentence before that: "I told you Friday, and I'm telling the honourable Judges now." follows the earlier statement about the "other soldiers did not take part." That seems to be what that is referring to. And then the following statement is: "I'm telling you now."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's confusing enough and probably should be left alone, and that's what I'll do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then there was the issue that developed over paragraph 45, and you'll recall this very well, where your statement says: "After we'd ordered a village to leave, within an hour it was like an atom bomb had hit the village. Soldiers were coming through the village and looting everything that was not nailed down." You said to Mr. Hannis in response to that question: "Now, what I told you on Friday - and I will repeat now in front of this honourable Trial Chamber - no one could carry anything with them, but it happened sometimes that an individual would come by. If it would have been a group, we would have seen them and they would have ended up in prison. And then I can guarantee that nobody could or was allowed to take anything with them throughout the war in Kosovo." Now, you say you told that to Mr. Hannis on Friday. Is that true, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then, finally, on the same subject at paragraph 46 -- or page 46, you were being asked about this by Judge Bonomy and said that you had not changed that paragraph before coming into court today. And your answer to Judge Bonomy on page 46 was: "I did clear this up with the Prosecutor. I told him on Friday literally that those were individuals, not a large group of people, if we don't take into account the last day." Is that true, that's what you told the Prosecutor on Friday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. Individuals did do such things. They didn't carry things because they couldn't carry things, but they looked for things they needed. As I said, there were people who were drug addicts and they looked for things. But on the last day there was looting and that's clear. That's beyond doubt. In the last days, there was looting and nobody could control it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've got your statement there. Could you look at paragraph 40, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At the very bottom of paragraph 40, what you say in your statement was that: "Looting by the VJ was strictly forbidden," and then you say "with the exception of the last day of our withdrawal." Now, when you say in paragraph 40 that looting by the VJ was strictly forbidden and then say what you said in paragraph 45 about soldiers taking everything that was not nailed down, one of those has to be wrong. One of those is true and one of them's not. And I take it it's your testimony today that looting was strictly forbidden and it didn't happen, as is set out in paragraph 45, that paragraph 45 was a mistake. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looting was forbidden, but on the last day there was no control. So there was looting. It was probably still prohibited, but it did go on. So until the unit could be kept under control until the last moment, there was no looting, with the exception of individual cases. On the last day, there was no longer any control. Yesterday, I explained that it could not be controlled. With the number of men the command had at their disposal, they could not prevent looting, so there was looting on the last day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I wasn't asking you about the last day, and please forget about that. In paragraph 40, you say: "Looting by the VJ was strictly forbidden;" and then in paragraph 45, you seem to describe wholesale looting by the VJ. Now, those both can't be true, and I think it's your position that paragraph 45 is not true, that that didn't happen as it is set out there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the characterisation of the question. It can be forbidden, but still happen. Also, he did not say it was VJ. He said soldiers, which is now explained that he meant individual soldiers, not the VJ as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ackerman, you've had the explanation already. The consistency -- the inconsistency we can see, but I think the witness has explained that there is substance in paragraph 45 but confined to individual instances. The only mass looting he acknowledges was on the last day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's the point I was trying to make, and I think it's made.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Witness, in paragraph 40 with regard to looting by the VJ being strictly forbidden, you even tell us about a Major Radic who was arrested for looting and put in prison. And that was confirmed with an exhibit that we saw yesterday. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that tends to confirm, doesn't it, your position that there was absolutely no tolerance for looting in the VJ during your time in Kosovo, until the time of the chaos of the last day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said just a little while ago. It was prohibited. I did say there were individual cases. Looting was banned, but there were some exceptions, just as there were these individuals. So this major did that and we arrested him and handed him over. So looting was forbidden; but on the last day, there was mass looting because there was no control. I think that's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, you were shown Exhibit P962 yesterday, or at least it was brought to the attention of the Chamber yesterday, that this list of charges brought against people from your battalion -- your brigade would show that there were several instances of arrests for looting. I don't want to take the time to go through it now today. I want to go to another subject, and this has to do with paragraph 37 of your statement. In that paragraph, you talk about searching houses in Djakovica in the neighbourhood of Cabrat. Can you describe in neighbourhood, this neighbourhood Cabrat, what kind of a neighbourhood was it. Was it a residential neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I assume you have not visited Djakovica, it's where the old barracks was, by the river. When you go by the church, Cabrat is on the left-hand side. That's the name of that neighbourhood in Djakovica. If you're coming from the direction of Belgrade, going through Djakovica, towards the church, it's on the right-hand side. So if you're coming from the direction of Pristina, it's on the right-hand side; and if you're coming from the other side, it's on the left-hand side. That is a residential neighbourhood called Cabrat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that residential neighbourhood is very next to the old barracks you say, very close?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the barracks is actually in Cabrat itself; it might be. There is a street running through. Djakovica ends with the barracks; and from the bridge onwards on the left-hand side, which is right next to the barracks, that's where the Cabrat neighbourhood in Djakovica begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that there was an exchange --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least, that's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you were there. If anybody knows, you probably do. You indicate there was an exchange of fire in one of the houses and one of the police inspectors was shot. Do you know who it was that shot this inspector? Was it KLA or what do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in that house, so I can't speculate. I know that a man was wounded, but how this came about I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Then in paragraph 38, you indicated that you withdrew from that residential neighbourhood because NATO bombs started dropping. Were bombs actually falling within the -- within that residential neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bombs were landing near the houses that were on fire, near those houses. I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it was the first time Djakovica was bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So because of that you and your group got out of there, and I assume a number of residents of that neighbourhood also departed because of the bombing that was going on there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't leave, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Your battalion, the location of your battalion, your assignment in your battalion, was along the Albanian border, was it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And are you familiar with the border posts that were manned by your battalion in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the border crossing to the Prizren -- the border post --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to Prizren, I didn't serve there so I don't know what the last border post is. But I crossed the border from Deva to Pastrik. I was at each of these positions, but I can't enumerate them all. On the right-hand side when you go, Deva is the first one and then the last one is I don't know. I can't remember now. This Cafa Prusit, Dejan Radanovic, I can't recall them all, but I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just let me have you look at an exhibit. It's P35 and it will come up on your screen, and I'll just ask you if you know where some of these border posts are. If you can find where they are, then I want you to draw a little square and we'll put some kind of a notation next to it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Ackerman, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot see this very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How's that? Can you see it better now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I see it, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know where the border crossing at Cafa Prusit was located? ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can we raise the map up just a little bit to go to the border. No, the other direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you see it now? You see Zub there. Do you see where Cafa Prusit was located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Zub, and I see Cafa Prusit written here as well, if that's it. Let me just find a pen. I see the village of Zub.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You just drew a red circle around the village of Zub, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And here is where the border crossing should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And you drew a red circle down below Zub. Would you put CP next to that, please. I need you to put the letters CP right next to that circle you made for Cafa Prusit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Very good. Now, do you know the border post at Dejan Radanovic? Do you know where that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if this is the border post, then it could only be here because it says, Dejan here -- no, it says Damjan here, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Ackerman, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I think we HAVE to zoom out a little bit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made a mistake, not Dejan Radanovic, or rather, I cannot see Dejan Radanovic here. But from Cafa Prusit, I think it's the next one on the right-hand side. When going from Djakovica, it's on the left-hand side. I was there, that's where the repeater was. They destroyed it, and I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Would it help you if we zoomed out a little bit, so you could see more of the map now, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It can't be done without losing the image, Mr. Ackerman. What do you want to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's go ahead and record this particular drawing.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC119, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last bit I draw is not Dejan Radanovic. It's not Dejan Radanovic, the last little circle I drew. It says Damjan here, and possibly that is one of the border posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's get a fresh map up there and zoom out a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Apparently, we've a technical problem which prevents us saving this at the moment, Mr. Ackerman. Can we move on and maybe come back to it again if necessary. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think what I might do is abandon this exercise and do it with some other witness, but there's a point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. It shouldn't even need a witness to establish the location of these various border posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll try and do it a different way, Your Honour, because this is obviously taking up time that I think at this point in time is unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, there were other border posts; Dejan Radanovic, border posts at Goden, that we can see on the map. Goden was there. There was one at Guri Bard and Velika Hoca, and Guri Bard and Deva?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Deva with a D.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. You know, don't you, that after the NATO bombing started on the 24th of March, these border posts came under frequent and rather constant attack, both by NATO aircraft and by KLA; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: NATO aircraft, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And KLA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From time to time, but I think that at Pastrik one was attacked. As for the others, well, sometimes there was some shooting but not constant shooting. NATO aircraft, though, every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know that Djakovica was within the operation zone of a KLA commander by the name of Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Later on I heard -- well, maybe I heard even then, but at that time the name didn't mean a thing to me. Well, now yes but not then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you know that just across the border in Albania from where your units were guarding the border was the town of Bajram Curri, which was a major departure point for arms smuggling and smuggling of KLA into Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, passing through the woods there near the border, we found a lot of material, some of it military material, some just things that were thrown away as people were fleeing. If that corroborates the Defence case, all right. I don't know what was in Bajram Curri. I know what was going on in the field. There was military equipment. There were civilian things that were discarded as they were fleeing. We found them in the forest. That was the case. But Bajram Curri, I don't know about that. Is this satisfactory? Is this what I can say now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't expect you to say any more than you know. This border area where Albania that your unit was tasked with defending, that was an area through which it was expected there may very well be a NATO ground attack, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, because of these frequent attacks by NATO, the communications links in your unit were not always functioning properly, were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost never; only in exceptional situations and very briefly at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And even when they were functioning, as you told us yesterday, they were not used after the NATO bombing started because of the possibility of revealing your locations or your communications to NATO and the enemy; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since the communication between the border posts and the command did exist, I assume that it was wire telephones or messengers. But since the commander toured the area every day, every day -- well, practically every day, in most cases I accompanied him. But I'm sure that every day he went from one border post to the other. So communications, very rarely and only in exceptional situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I have given you a document in a black folder there this morning. That's Prosecution Exhibit, and it is the war diary of your battalion. And it is written by hand and --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, I did not see the diary when it was written because it was not within the scope of my work. I cannot say anything, when it was written, by who, under what circumstances, nothing, nothing more than this. So probably it was written by the person who signed it, and I don't know whether he wrote it. I don't know under what conditions. I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, those are -- you've just answered a whole bunch of questions I didn't ask you. It's handwritten, and I want you to see if you can find the entry for the 30th of March. It starts with the 24th of March, so the 30th of March should be fairly soon after the beginning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 29th, I found it. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The last entry there for the 30th of March says: "During the day, about 2.000 people crossed the Cafa Prusit border crossing. Transport for the children and the elderly was organised. The Djakovica-Prizren road is jammed by refugee columns. No other sight is so distressing as a view of the column of the poor who have been forced to leave their houses. The soldiers simply couldn't resist giving the children fruit juices and biscuits as they passed by." Now, do you have any knowledge of the soldiers giving people that kind of assistance, juice, biscuits, and how distressing this was to people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't only that; it wasn't only that. I -- oh. Could I have a bit of water, please. Just some water, just a little bit of water, please. Could somebody give me some water, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could the usher deal with that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was by the post office in Djakovica. I saw a woman whose children were crying and she needed diapers for them, and I asked the woman in the shop to give her diapers. Our commander had a check-point at the exit out of Brekovac where people got everything they needed; water, bread, whatever they needed, literally, everything they needed. The check-point was there for as long as it was needed while the column was moving on, so it was just a day, a day and a half. A lot of people went through, and it was a terrible sight to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I will tell you that this diary is signed by your major, and that part that I just read to you, if it was indeed written by him, would you say that it was representative --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite true, fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- representative of what was going on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is fully correct, fully correct, and it's not only him. It was really sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 43 of your statement, you talk about relocating people from the village of Zub, and there was a VJ command post there at the time, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you know that --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got there, it was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you know that NATO was targeting VJ command posts, VJ observation posts, VJ border posts. All VJ installations were being targeted by NATO; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But our command post, the old one, where we were the first time, had not been hit. It was the house of an Albanian where he lived, too, until we all left. When we left, he left with us, towards Djakovica. The yard -- well, it was this one yard. He and his family lived in one house, and the command post was in the other house. The commander, the deputy commander, the security organ, in fact, the staff of the battalion was in that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want you to stay with that diary with me now and go to the entry for April 2nd; and a moment ago when we were looking at the map, we saw the villages down below, Zub, Goden, and Zulfaj down near the border. To your knowledge, Goden and Zulfaj were located near the border and near some VJ posts, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't really understand what you asked me. I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The villages of Goden and Zulfaj, these were located in the border area near a VJ border post, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, but I no longer remember that. It's been a long time. Well, I heard of these villages; but as for their position, I could not say exactly where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it you'd agree if there were instances where villagers were actively assisting NATO or the KLA by providing information, by providing light signals, by directing bombing, that it would have made sense to relocate the people from those villages, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that, and I cannot talk about that. That was done by some other people who were in charge of that. I remember that from our position in Zub, I watched these light signals from the direction of Djakovica towards the sky. And we were trying to find where they were coming from, and we searched a building the next day. It was a state building. I can't remember what it was, but we didn't find anything there. On the following day, we didn't really touch anyone but we just searched the building. We didn't find anything there. I know that we could see these signals from those villages, but there is nothing I can really say about this. I cannot decide about that. I am not involved in that. Other people decide about this. I am not involved in any way, this way or that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At the April 2nd entry in that diary, the last two entries, the first one says: "Because of sending light signals and hostile behaviour, the villages of Goden and Zulfaj were evacuated." So apparently they found out where it was coming from and dealt with it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The last sentence is: "The unit is hastily carrying out engineering work in the defence sector." Now, I presume that engineering work was in preparation for a possible ground attack. Am I right about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that there were engineering works running along parallel lines, parallel to the border, that is. Well, I cannot say for sure, but I think it went on for a long time and it was very long. It was really done by the Roma. They worked on it, say, 15 days or so, and that's not an exaggeration. It was the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We talked about these border posts being attacked by NATO and also by the KLA. I'd like you to look at the entry in that diary now for the 18th of April, and the last entry at --?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- indicates that -- last entry at --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not managed to find this. I cannot find that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 18 April.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go ahead. Go ahead and read it because I can't read this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It says: "The pioneer squad in the Goden border post sector came under fire from the territory of the Republic of Albania." And my question is if they came under fire from the Republic of Albania, would that have been KLA that was firing at them from Albania?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what it is that I'm going to say to you now. There was an attack at Pastrik, but I don't know what date that was. I was walking towards the KLA. I, with my group, was walking in the direction of the KLA, and Captain Rangelov was walking with us to show us the road and then a platoon of military police was behind us. And a day before that, or rather, the previous night a scout got killed. So perhaps that is it. I'm not sure. Perhaps that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the force of my question - and without going into them, there are a number of entries in this diary about coming under fire from the Republic of Albania - and I just wonder if you can tell us whether that would have been fire by the KLA from the Republic of Albania or were the -- was the Albanian military actually attacking the Serb border posts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were all sorts of things going on there. The KLA and -- well, the Albanian army, they did not appear in any big numbers, very few people, one, two men, and then probably they shot at soldiers and then they would retreat. They have better roads when you cross the border there into Albania. At that area there was a bunker, an Albanian bunker, every 50 metres, and there are at least three roads leading to every one of these bunkers. So they would shoot and they would simply retreat. Now, both were shooting, sometimes the KLA, sometimes the other ones; but at any rate, it wasn't that it was the Albanian army that was attacking in large numbers. It would be a small group. They would shoot, and they would run away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least that's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to digress just for a moment from this because there's an entry on the 27th of April in that diary, and you might find the 27th after April. And I want to ask you about that entry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it. I cannot read it, though. I'm looking for it, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This talks about the 27th of April at the -- near the Korenica-Meja village -- actually, Meja Orize. And it says this: "At 0835 hours in the cemetery sector along the blockade axis." Do you know where the cemetery sector along the blockade axis was located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I know what you're talking about. The cemetery was in Brekovac on the other side of the river, as I explained yesterday. So it wasn't on the side where the blockade was, but it was across the river on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. And what the diary says is that someone from a group of civilians, among whom were children, fired at the soldiers manning the blockade. Two soldier volunteers were wounded, that was Vuckovic and Lapadatovic. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lapadatovic, well, sir, I talked to them. I talked to these men when they were wounded, and I talked to the people who were with them. And it would really be a great shame for me to lie and say that civilians shot at them. It wasn't that the police were targeting them, but the police were shooting and they hit them. As they told me then, the civilians could not have been shooting because I was with these civilians. I was on the road when these civilians were passing by. I was with them then. So then I would have had to see, had they been shooting, or they would have shot at me, as I was the closest person there and the medical people were there, too. And those who lived by the river, I don't think that they knew where they were, let alone be in a position to shoot.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to go to the entry in that diary now for the 5th of May. Yes, I found it here. As I said a few moments ago, I cannot read a thing. I can tell you about what happened if I remember what happened, but I cannot read this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you if you knew about this, or if you know generally about this. The diary reports that at 1345 hours on the 5th of May, the observation post from the Guri Bard sector reported that ten tanks and 50 soldiers with seven motor vehicles had arrived in the Nikolici village sector. Now, the Nikolici village sector is in Albania. What were these tanks? Who did those tanks belong to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there then. I was there -- well, I don't know whose tanks they were. We saw them pass by. I went there to see what was going on. I went there with my commander then, and I saw what was going on. The military was later tasked, and then they went there and came back the following day. But I know that they appeared for sure, and I think this was a pure provocation to see how our people would react. It is true that the tanks came. I was there at the time, and I saw the tanks come.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm nearly finished. I could probably finish within ten minutes or we could break now. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's better to break, Mr. Ackerman. We'll go into closed session while the witness leaves the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I want to skip ahead a bit. I want to go to the diary entry for the 17th of May.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the diary you gave me as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's the one.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You will -- you will notice there's a report that at 1520 hours we observed nine tanks and ten trucks in the sector of the Caz village. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now; but if there were tanks, then I certainly heard them. But I can't be sure now, so I cannot tell you whether there were or not any provocations. But there were provocations with tanks and with infantry, only I can't remember the date. I know that there were such provocations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the next entry between 1705 and 1720, it says: "Two tanks followed by infantry fired on the position of the second," something or other, "in the sector of Cafa Prusit. After opening fire from 120-millimetre mortar and 155-howitzers, one tank moved back to the sector of TT-186, and the infantry went away and the tank that was hit burst into flames." So there was an actual battle that took place with those tanks in Albania at Cafa Prusit apparently on that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of that, but I wasn't there when it happened. I have heard about it. I wasn't on the spot, but I did hear that it happened. At the time I think I was at Pastrik. I can't be sure, but I think I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then later on that day at 1740, six tanks were seen in the sector of Dobruna village. So there seems to have been quite a lot of tank activity across the border in Albania that day, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what it says in the diary, yes, but the provocations occurred on a daily basis. Sometimes it was infantry or vehicles or tanks or this or that, but for the most part it was every day. This was the only possible route where they could possibly go with tanks towards Kosovo in that area, so probably they were testing their strength. Who can know? But I think that's what it was. There were daily provocations, sometimes with vehicles, sometimes with tanks. I heard about this, but I wasn't there then. I heard there was shooting, but I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'm not going to take you through any more of these incidents of attacks on these border posts. As you've just said, it was a daily thing, it was an incessant thing, and it's in this exhibit for the Chamber to see. What I will ask you now is: It's the case, isn't it, that these constant attacks, both by NATO and from across the border in Albania, had a bad effect on the morale of the troops that were manning those border posts, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the only problem was having a bath at the border post. Everything else was bearable. The border posts were destroyed, and the troops had nowhere to take a bath, and that was the biggest problem. As for the provocations, they happened every day and one got used to them, so they didn't bother us. Baths were the biggest problem. The border posts were destroyed, but everything else was bearable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for morale, I'm not sure it was bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I asked you that question because of an entry that appears in the diary for the 7th of June, where it says: "In our regular combat report we informed the superiors," I don't know what that translation is, "that the situation in the units is very difficult. The troops are exhausted and morale is falling." And that's the reason I asked you that question, just so you know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, we withdrew from there on the 8th, if I remember correctly. We already knew then. The people I talked to - I won't go into any political decisions made by the command or the decision to withdraw - but I and the people who were there, we were not happy about withdrawing from Kosovo. We were absolutely against withdrawal at any cost. We were prepared to stay until the end, until the last man.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I had asked you about the concern that there was going to be a NATO ground attack across that border area that your battalion was responsible for, and there is some information in this diary on the 5th and 6th of May. The -- I'm just going to share it with you and ask you for some comment. On the 5th of May at 1019 hours, enemy aircraft attacked the area north-west of Djakovica. At 1345, the observation post from the Guri Bard sector reported that ten tanks and 50 soldiers had arrived across the border. We talked about that a moment ago. At 1730 to 1930, aircraft launched a heavy attack against the battalion defence sector using rockets and cluster bombs. At 1830, four rockets were fired in the Kuzliu [phoen] village sector, kitchen was hit. A private was killed. At 1925 hours, cluster bombs were fired on the Cafa Prusit border post. A sergeant was killed. Two soldiers were wounded. At 20 --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- hours there was enemy infantry fire on their positions in Cafa Prusit, and that was activity that was going on all along that border on the 5th of May; and then if you look at the 6th of May, after another enemy aircraft cluster bomb fired in the Pastrik sector, there was an alert sounded for all units because a general attack from land and air was announced. Do you remember that alert that was given that day about an imminent ground attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Pastrik then. I wasn't afraid of the land attack. I didn't care whether it would happen today, tomorrow, or whenever. I went to Kosovo with one goal, and I didn't care whether they would attack or not. If they attacked, I would be there; if they didn't attack, I would still be there. It was quite clear as far as the troops were concerned that they would defend at any cost.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, in -- I appreciate that answer. It really didn't have anything to do with my question. My question was: There was serious belief that there was going to be a ground attack from Albania and there were some indications of that, that fortified that belief, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The night between the 5th and the 6th, I went to Pastrik. There was an air-raid warning. A group had crossed over. There's a big rock in that area, and my commander and I had been there for a while and the commander who was there assured us that everything was all right. Maybe he, may commander that is, wrote this down somewhere. However, it turned out they had no troops there. They had been lying to us. And that's why I went there that night, as I said, in order to fight back if they should start coming towards us, towards Prizren, to be there. But they remained at that rock and didn't go further inland, inwards. There was an alert. I know what you're asking me about. I was not afraid of any attack, nor were the people I was with. They could attack any time they wanted. We were not afraid. If you're satisfied with that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I know you're not afraid. I wasn't trying to prove that you were afraid. I want to go now to one very brief last subject with you, and that's back to the Korenica-Meja area on the 27th of April, when you were there at the crossroads with your major. What I'm wondering was how was it you happened to be there with your major that day. Where was your lieutenant and the rest of your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. You put your question badly. I was not at the crossroads with the major. We had a command post between the crossroads and the village. It was 80 or a hundred metres away from the crossroads on the right-hand side of the road. There was a derelict old house and an old outhouse where we were, so we were not at the crossroads. I was then securing the commander. I was his body-guard. The others were with the other soldiers, and I was with the commander according to the daily order, providing security for him with a few other men and another man who was from my group.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Where was your lieutenant and the rest of your group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lieutenant was not there, but the rest of the group were in the creek, as I explained to His Honour when we were saying that we were there to prevent the KLA from leaving the village, not the civilians. The creek running from that crossroads up the hill to the right. It's not in the map. That's the road, that is. It's a road used by carts mainly. It's a dirt road, so it's probably not in the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. When you -- when you told your major after you had checked it out that people were being killed, you told us yesterday and also in your statement that that made him very angry. But you also have no information that he reported to anybody up the chain of command what you had told him. You don't know whether he did that or not, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't check what the commander is doing, perhaps that day or another day or at that time. But at that point in time, I wasn't checking what he was doing and that wasn't my task. He was the commander. He should be checking on me, not I on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that. My -- I wonder if you happened to report what you had seen to your lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He wasn't there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After you had reported to your major about what you saw, he then ordered you and one other soldier to provide an escort for a group of people out of that area to Djakovica to protect them, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was after those two people were wounded that you read about in the previous paragraph. There's a field between the village and the place where we were, and we saw that they were ready to go and there was shooting everywhere. There was general chaos. The troops were on the right -- on the left-hand side of the road, and he ordered me to go with that soldier and evacuate those people to Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And the position that you've taken in your statement at least is that if we had not done this, if we had not protected them, they would have never gotten past the check-point and the men would certainly not be alive. So it's your position that you and your major by those actions saved the lives of a number of people that day, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my opinion. It's still my opinion today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And after that day, paragraph 66 of your statement, you tell us that none of your unit or any of the soldiers that you knew were satisfied with what happened that day. "We were annoyed that we were made a part of what these police had decided to do."
