Actually, the VJ soldiers that you knew were very surprised and distressed with what they learned happened that day, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening, we were given the task that we were supposed to carry out in the morning, and such things were not discussed. He was absolutely surprised. There was no talk about this. There was talk about combing the terrain to see there were no KLA there, but this was something quite different. And I assert that my commander was surprised by what happened because I -- I had known him since, I'm not sure, but I think since 1992. He was very surprised by the event that occurred. I assume that he did not know it would happen. I'm almost sure he did not know it would happen, in view of his reaction. I assume that even the police command didn't know what was happening on the ground, because their officers were not there either, except for just the policemen, but no senior officers. And they were on the bridge, not on the ground, where they should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it wasn't just your major, your commander, that was angry and disgusted about what happened, but all the VJ soldiers you knew were angry and embarrassed and disgusted by what happened, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people I was in communication with that day, yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think we will get through this cross-examination very quickly because my colleague, Mr. Ackerman, has already asked many of the questions I was planning to put.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. K90, my name is Mihajlo Bakrac. I'm one of the Defence counsel of General Lazarevic. As I said, my colleague, Mr. Ackerman, has already put many of the questions I was going to put, so I believe we can get through my part of the cross-examination very quickly. What I wish to clarify is whether you can tell us what the establishment title was of the unit you were in during the war in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 2nd Battalion of the 549th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, but your unit. Just a second, please. You were questioned by counsel who spoke English up to now. Now we are going to have a problem because we both speak the same language, so we have to make a break. When you see on your monitor that the transcript has stopped, then you can start your answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was part of the military police platoon. Did you hear my reply? It was -- a military police platoon has three squads, so we were an extra squad of the military police platoon. The military police company was in Prizren, and we were a forward platoon in Djakovica. We were part of that platoon, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you remember who the commander was of that platoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a second lieutenant, but I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you recall the date when exactly you joined this military police platoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 27th in the evening, I arrived in Kosovo. It's in my military booklet -- no -- oh, yes, yes, that's right. On the 27th, I was in Zub at the command post. My commander met us there and told us what I repeated yesterday. This is neither Kosovo [as interpreted] nor Bosnia. Here orders will be respected. He said that orders were sacred and should not be deviated from, in spite of the fact we were volunteers. This happened on the 27th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Bakrac. Could we briefly, please, go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just for the record, paragraph [sic] 49, line 19, again it appears, "this is neither Kosovo nor Bosnia." I know the witness corrected that yesterday, that he meant to say Croatia nor Bosnia, and I'm sure that's what he meant today, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Croatia, that's right, that's right. I do apologise. Thank you, gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, in the war diary in the entry there, it says that on the 3rd of April, 1999, the arrival of 22 volunteers is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were already there when they arrived. They arrived after we did, and they went to the Deva border post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let's clarify something else from your statement. You said that Nesovic was a security officer in the battalion. Is it correct that he does not have any command responsibility in that position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He doesn't have his men. The platoon commander does. But he, as the security organ, doesn't have his men, his soldiers, to whom they are the direct superiors, as far as I can remember, except for a courier and a driver and so on. They don't have any active-duty soldiers, so the lieutenant didn't have any soldiers he commanded personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So we can assume that he was simply directing security measures?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the whole battalion, he was coordinating between the brigade commander and security in the battalion. That's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. My colleague Mr. Ackerman has already asked you, and you tried to find this on the sketch. I would just like to try and pin-point a certain location. Is it correct that the area of responsibility of our battalion stretched from the Likan border post from Pastrik to Kosare and that this was the front line which was about 30 kilometres long?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 37, approximately, and the depth was -- if the border belt was five kilometres wide - and you will recall that I think in 1998 or 1999 the border belt was moved by certain distance. I can't remember exactly how much - then that's it. That was the area we covered, nothing beyond, only the border and the border belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But in order to save time and for you to be able to go home sooner, you said the border belt was moved. Will you agree with me that in 1999 while you were there, the border belt was widened to ten kilometres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how wide exactly. We didn't have ten kilometres everywhere, but in certain places, yes, from the border to a village. If I was in a village where there was a command post, that was supposed to be the barracks and there was a barracks in Djakovica. But, of course, we couldn't be there because it had been destroyed. We were at the forward command post, that could be between one and five kilometres. It would all depend on the distance, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but has the Court understood?.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Understood what, Mr. Bakrac -- sorry, understood what, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you understand what I was trying to say? The distance between the border and the place in that ten kilometres that counsel asked me about, in some places it was one kilometre, in other places five 5. It was up to ten kilometres, so it was not beyond a 10-kilometre belt. It did not go beyond that distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We understand your answer. We doubt if it's what -- it's the answer that Mr. Bakrac anticipated, but let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the next question will make things clearer. Sir, can we agree that the area of defence of the battalion was such that at least 90 percent of your battalion, of your unit, was along the state border in that area of the state border, except for a small part of the rear that was behind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said 70 percent in my statement. Viewed from this distance in terms of the actual kilometres, well, we never had enough troops at the border and everywhere. So it is possible that even that number that you said is correct. So in my statement I wrote 70 percent. You asked me about 90 percent, so I do allow for that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Percentages are not important. If I understood you correctly, you had a lack of troops. So, basically, you were all in the border belt except for a small contingent in the rear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, today they would be here and tomorrow they would be elsewhere. When something was needed, then they would go wherever necessary. There was no surplus, let's put it that way. Usually, the military police is not deployed anywhere in such situations. This was an exception. So the military police platoon was deployed in Pastrik at the border itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, will you agree with me that all the soldiers got a pocket brochure containing instructions based on the Geneva Conventions and Rules of Conduct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received that. I had that. But I know, because I worked in the military, and when I trained soldiers we trained them about that, too. Now, I forgot how it goes exactly, but we worked on that. This was done on a compulsory basis whenever troops were brought in. I don't know whether all the soldiers had it, but I had this. I'm not sure, perhaps I still have this paper at home with the leaflets that I collected that were thrown from NATO aircraft. I stored all of this. I think I still have it at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. With my colleague Mr. Ackerman, you've already dealt with the situation pertaining to NATO bombing and cluster bombs. But can we agree that throughout, from the beginning of the war through April and May in particular, in terms of the deployment of your unit, there were almost everyday attacks by NATO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You cannot put it that way. If we take into account that the tower that is between our command post in Brekovac and the old barracks is at a 100-metre distance and that same tower was bombed at least ten times every day, all units -- well, there's not a single position of our battalion that was not bombed at least twice in a day, and sometimes even more than that, ten, 12. Depending on the situation, there was not a single hour, a single hour, that we were not bombed. Even an hour is a lot. It was more than that. We had the impression that all the aircraft that were flying back from Albania did not discharge all of their bombs would throw them on us before flying back to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly when you said yesterday about a few villages -- well, actually you made a correction there that were relocated, that practically moved out, relocated towards Djakovica. The villages closer to Djakovica. These were villages that were from that border area and from the area of responsibility of your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman asked me about these villages and the names. I remember Zub. I remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not interested in names. I'm --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- only villages in that area. The first villages near Djakovica. There were one or two or three villages that had already left. They were totally empty, or rather, the people had left. When I came there, they were empty. I don't know about them. For these that were here, for sure I know when I was there they had gone to the area of Djakovica, and not to Albania. What happened to these people later on, whether they went further on, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we agree that the reason for this relocation is precisely this, everyday bombing and the danger of a land invasion, a ground invasion in that border area and that many villages left on their own in the area of Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't put it that way because had we stayed there and had we expelled people from there, it would only be us; and then they would have only targeted us and nobody would be crazy to do that. So these people were there, and they went together with us, towards town, closer. That would be it. The command knew about this better, and they were the ones who decided about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you. Do you know as well - and I think it is stated in the war diary of your battalion - that the border villages in Albania; namely, Vlahna, Dobruna, Zogaj, that civilians from those villages also moved out and relocated precisely because they were so close to the border and because of the bombing and possible land offensive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the name of the village near Cafa Prusit is near -- on the Albanian side, that is, but I saw through binoculars several times and knew it was empty. There were no inhabitants there. Sometimes a man or two men would come with rifles, but not more than that. So the village was empty. For what reason? Well, probably because these people would sometimes miss and not all the bombs would fall on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it also correct - we have already heard that you are not afraid and that you were not afraid of fighting and we believe that, indeed - but can we say that at the border post of Kosare, there was practically combat every day and conflicts every day and attempts made to get through that border post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there for two days only, only two days. There were constant attacks, air attacks, constantly, quite literally. Every moment there were attacks. There is some trees where you can seek shelter, and in other areas there is some kind of bushes. It is very inaccessible. Well, I don't know, but we were prepared for every eventuality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you haven't answered the question. It was -- you were asked if there were actual conflicts there every day, and I don't think that's a reference to NATO bombing. It's a reference to something else. And you were there for two days, so what happened in those two days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at that time I saw my neighbour get killed. He was an active-duty soldier. I saw that a man was being taken by a tractor, and I looked and it was Marinko, this young man from the same neighbourhood that I live in. And there were constant conflicts, therefore, between members of the KLA and our forces, our army, every day plus NATO bombing, which was constant without cessation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said to us just now that there was constant fighting with the KLA. Was there a danger of the fall of Kosare to lead to a link-up of the KLA from the Carragojs valley and the area of Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, listen, if that were to happen, that is a flat land. I assume -- well, if we look at it -- if you go down from Kosare to Junik, on the left-hand side is Decani and the area towards Pec. Well, I guess that is the way it would be, but then I cannot claim either this or that. But people who are more knowledgeable about this probably would know what would happen. You see what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm interested in whether we will agree that in view of all the facts that we have referred to just now, the blockade along the border belt held by the army that you explained yesterday was fully justified from a military point of view.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I think that we even had too few troops at the border. If we knew what kind of enemy we were up against, because we knew that a possible infantry attack, combined forces of NATO and the Albanians, the KLA, would be there. So it's a lot of people. And equipment -- well, I had the impression that we even had too few people on the force there, because this was just what would happen had it happened. But it was my impression that the units that were there on the border itself, it would be hard for us. Well, we would fight up to a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I understand, but I just needed to deal with this question. There is no need to go on. Well, again, the diary that was proffered by the Prosecutor. Is it correct that, for example, on the 23rd of April during the search of the area of Romel Lukanje [phoen], six KLA members were taken prisoner in uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I did not see these people, but I did see some black uniforms and I saw insignia. I saw rifles in the military police platoon. Now, whose uniforms they were, who wore them, and whose weapons these were, I don't know about that. I saw a list. When we are on duty there, then it is stated what weapons were seized. Do you remember what I said to the Prosecutor? One of these men had committed an offence and then they detained him and then his weapons were there in the military police platoon. There were uniforms there; but who wore them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, in relation to that, is it correct that according to combat rules it is compulsory for a unit, before it takes up positions, to search the terrain and to see whether there are hostile troops there, mines, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you're going to position your unit there and if you do not secure the terrain there before that, then you've made a mistake, especially in wartime. If you take up a certain part of the area and if you had not searched it earlier on, well, what can happen is that somebody slaps you around later. That is compulsory. Any army in the world does it. It wasn't only us. It's logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, do you know that in the night between the 27th and 28th of April, and when you were talking about Meja and Korenica, that it is precisely through the positions of the military police platoon the KLA tried to get through and that group was destroyed on that occasion, that KLA group. I think it's the village of Racaj. Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. Maybe it did happen. Sorry, but I really don't remember. Sorry. Well, there are a lot of things that you asked me about, and it's been quite a while and I don't remember quite a few things. Possibly that did happen, but I don't remember. I remember -- well, it's not contained in my statement, but I remember that there was this misunderstanding with a man who was shooting at military policemen, but that man ran away. Now, I don't know who he was or what he was like. Nothing happened to him. They started firing at him and he fled across the river. That's to say -- I don't know really.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted) I would like to ask you about the day when the column from Korenica went by the place where you were with the commander.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, we had no contacts with these people, no contacts whatsoever, absolutely no contacts with them. I had contact when I went to get those who were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I understand. We don't have to repeat what you've already said. I understand. The army, quite simply, held the line vis-a-vis the border.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the left side of the road leading to Junik, between the crossroads that I drew and the entrance into the village, nothing more than that, and the part of the brook that I added later on. Nothing else. We did not have more than 100 men there because we could not bring reinforcements from anywhere. So it was us there, we from the military police, and part of the soldiers from the Deva border post, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And very briefly, I think that we're going to finish within five minutes or so. When we talk about the incident on that day, is it correct that Vukadinovic [phoen] drove an ambulance and took them to Djakovica, that was staff sergeant Vukadinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. If you were to bring in a thousand people here, I would recognize him, but I don't know what his name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I asked you about this so that we would --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, possibly Vukadinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know Staff Sergeant Vukadinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, possibly it was that man. I am not sure. I know who the man is, but I cannot remember name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Since you know who it is, Vukadinovic that is, do you know that as for the hamlet of Cufodoj [phoen], he took ten Albanian families into his own house that was in that hamlet? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about it, but it wouldn't surprise me. We had a very fair relationship with people in the place that we're talking about, because I said in my statement that the Territorial Defence major guaranteed for these people that they would never create any problems. And as far as we were concerned, the military, we didn't go there at all. We had regular patrols near Deva and towards this other place on the other side of Deva. We never entered their villages, absolutely never.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, thank you. My last question: It is very important for us to clarify something. In the additional piece of information, there is something that I'm going to ask you about, and I am sure that my learned friend Mr. Hannis omitted to ask you this by accident. When he asked you about B, the killing of an elderly civilian, an old civilian man, is it correct that you also said to Mr. Hannis that the major did not know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite correct, absolutely correct, from word -- every single word is correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the second lieutenant knew, the one I didn't want to mention. Those were orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, a part of that passage --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the honourable Trial Chamber and to Mr. Hannis. It's my last question, so perhaps I wasn't as cautious as I should be, but it's a good thing that we can correct it. I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I have questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown P2019, page 4. Your Honour, I just need to say something. The Prosecutor -- 2573 is another document that the Prosecutor proffered, but I think that 2019 and 2573 are one and the same document. So I'm going to use the same number that Mr. Ackerman used, that is to say 2019, so that I would not lead to any confusion when analysing all of this later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to those two documents, there is one difference. They both purport to be the war diary of the 2nd Battalion, and the difference is on the last page. I think, on the version that I offered I think 2019, it has the signature of the commander. The other version, which I was -- I think was received from the Commission on Cooperation or else brought in through General Delic, the signature block is covered up with -- with something that's in B/C/S that I can't read, and I don't know if I have the English translation. But I think it's some kind of certification from the commission. Now, I assume they're the same to the extent I've been able to compare the two B/C/S versions. They seem to be identical. That's the reason for the difference and I offered the one that had the signature block.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's 2573, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I think that's 2019.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 2019, that's fine. Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will use 2573, or rather, 2019 because we have it translated into English. If only the image would not be broadcast, I would put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is the war diary of your motorised brigade, which says that under the 29th of March by order of the 549th Motorised Brigade command, 122-millimetre [as interpreted] mortar platoon was sent to the Velika Hoca sector - I won't read out the name of the commander - and was subordinated to BG 6 of the 549th Motorised Brigade. My question is: Within your battalion, did you have a 120-millimetre mortar platoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The man whose name you didn't read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please, just answer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- is he a Gorani? I can see that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please just answer the question. It's a simple question. I don't know why Mr. Visnjic even referred to the name. Just let's get to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. There were mortars. I don't know whether they were part of our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could the witness be shown page 6 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While that's coming up, Your Honour, for clarity's sake I should indicate one other difference between 2593 [sic] and 2019 is that in 2593 [sic], the pages were copied one at a time; and on 2019, the full open diary was copied, so one page contains two pages of the diary. So as long as Mr. Visnjic refers to the dates of the entry we should be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I take it the reference to 2593 was to 2573.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. I was thinking of Vasiljevic, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one page before. The Serbian version is on the right page, but in English it's the previous page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Sir, the date is the 3rd of April, 1999. I will read you that entry. The first line says: "The unit established lateral contact in the general area of the village of Zub. The 122-millimetre mortar platoon returned from the task by 1800 hours."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the general area of the village of Zub?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, let me put the question if possible.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Are you aware, or rather, does this date correspond to the date when part of your battalion returned from the Orahovac area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. What I do know is that these soldiers with the mortars - I can't remember the exact date - arrived in Zub, and they were deployed in a house which was on the edge of the village next to the creek running towards the border. That's all I can tell you, and you know why? Because a neighbour of mine was an active-duty soldier in that platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my questions refer to transcript page 9144, 9171, 9177, and 9205. This was the testimony of another witness at this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Sir, you said you don't remember what your platoon commander was. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was a second lieutenant, but I don't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And who was the squad leader?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the situation, it was I, when I was here; and he, when he was there. So when I wasn't there, it was him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat your answer to my question who the squad leader --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you make a pause after my question and then tell me who your squad commander was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we can go into closed session, if he's going to name his squad commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it appears that these are unsigned, unsworn statements of individuals who were in the bigger unit that this witness was a part of, and I think they're going to be used to impeach this witness about his whereabouts and some of his other testimony. I don't have a problem with them serving as the basis for asking a question, but I don't want this to be used as a backdoor to get in statements of individuals who aren't here to be cross-examined. That's my concern. And if he's going to put that up as an exhibit to show to this witness, I oppose to that procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, what's your response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to take responsibility for some of these statements. 3D502 is signed. The other statements, apart from 3D500, were taken by telephone by the investigator. Our problem was that in order to save time, we sent unsigned copies for translation, and by chance it was the unsigned versions that were put into the system as soon as the translations were received. By the end of today, I can obtain 3D502 with a signature, 3D500 with a signature, and the other three that I intend to use, 501, 499, and 504 are signed by the investigator who conducted the telephone interview with the witness. I did not intend to use any of these exhibits now but later, but I thought I should clarify this right away. I wanted 3D26 put on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you appreciate, Mr. Visnjic, that they don't become evidence in the case simply by putting them to the witness in this context. And what you're really doing is putting points to him that come from these statements. They're the basis for you posing these questions. So it would probably be better if you were able to deal with this without exhibiting -- or without bringing it on to the screen, the actual exhibit, and putting the points you want to put to the witness. And if there is something that needs the statement to be seen for the purpose of challenging his evidence, then that can be done as necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll try to do that in that way. Could we have 3D26.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Sir, this map is in colour. Do you see it first of all? Does this territory correspond to the territory you sketched in IC118?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown page 3 of this exhibit. This is the same map only enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark on this map the place where you say your command post was located and the place where you say your platoon, or rather, your platoon was under siege.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you put a letter A next to the line showing where your platoon was under siege. When I say "your platoon," I mean the police platoon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't just the police. It was also the command platoon. There was some soldiers from the border and us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And who was at this other line that you drew here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My squad.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So your squad was --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Holding that part of the creek here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This whole area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not the whole area. It's -- I mean, it's 400 metres, 300 or 400 metres. It's not a big area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How far was your squad from the command post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 150 metres, 150 to 200 metres, not more, from the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So your squad was 150 metres from the command post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 150 to 200 metres, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And how far was the police from your command post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police was at the crossroads here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how far away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 80 to a hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So, If I understand correctly, your squad was --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Behind the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: -- 50 metres behind the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the creek, at the end of that yard where that building was uphill along the creek, that's where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And it was just your squad, just ten men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ten men, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And from the place where your squad was, could one see the road and the command post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: From the place where your squad was, could you see the command post of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, because there was a creek and then a road; and then across the road in this part here, in this area here, there is one, two, three houses here, and then a compound of buildings which I marked on my sketch.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please wait for us to ask you before you mark something, because it will be very chaotic if you keep marking it. Could you please tell me the following now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please assign an IC number to this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, could you explain what you now understand this exhibit now shows. What does A represent?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in my understanding, A is a part of the witness's unit which was blocking the road, or rather, it was next to it. The other line that was drawn represents the blockade line held by his squad. Between the two, there are dots. According to the witness's testimony, they should represent some houses and the spot where the police were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The police were --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please put an X where the police were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why are we on a different plan from the diagram on the statement of the witness? Why have we moved on to something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when you compare both exhibits, and it was my intention, we'll see that some places on the map are located in different places, in different spots, and I would like the witness to explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But when he was asked: "Can you put a letter A next to the line showing where your platoon was under siege," and he then says: "It wasn't just the police, it was also the command platoon." "And who was at this other line that you draw at?" So, he puts A where his platoon is supposed to be under siege, but do you understand that there was someone under siege on the road?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't think we could follow this evidence with this diagram as part of it. So if you want this to be clear, I think you should start again with a fresh copy of this and we shouldn't mark this. We should start again with clear questions of the witness. Don't let him speak over you. Control what he's doing so that we can see exactly what's being put on the diagram. And it looks as though today's not going to end this evidence now, if my information about anticipated

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us try again. 3D26, page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Witness K90, please listen to me carefully. First draw a line to mark the position of your squad in the blockade.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you place the number 1 next to it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now draw another line to show where the rest of your battalion in the blockade was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you put the number 2 there just below.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now please mark the spot where the command post of your battalion was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Please put the number 3 there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you also mark the spot where the police were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone was not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you please put the number 4 next to the circle.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. [Interpretation] I think we could assign an IC number to this exhibit now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's now much clearer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've got the same problem as before, Mr. Visnjic. Do you need something else on the screen just now or can you carry on until we wait while a technician comes and photographs this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can ask the witness for another location that he could introduce into the map and while we're waiting for the technician.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be IC120, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Problem solved. Carry on, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The place where the other two soldiers were wounded, the ones you mentioned in your testimony of yesterday and today, could that place be seen from the command post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What do you think, how far was that place from your command post of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you for sure how far it was, but one could not see it with the naked eye; not because it would be so far, too far to see, but, rather, you couldn't see it because of the terrain. There was a road going through from the entrance to the village and then turns towards the river, to the left. That's where they were, and that's why you couldn't see them from the command post. But it wasn't too far to see with the naked eye. It was simply the configuration of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I right to say that communication between the platoons and the command post was via RUP-12 radio devices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I don't remember. In some other situations, probably; but on that occasion, I'm pretty sure they were not used, although don't hold me to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did each and every commander also have a Motorola?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which commanders?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Platoon commanders.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that is true, but they were not using them at that time because there were planes flying constantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: According to (redacted) be wounded. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How did you learn of that if you were at the command post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Someone came over to tell us that, but I can't recall who. I think that's the way it was, although I'm unsure. Someone came over to tell us that he was wounded. There is a possibility that it was communicated via other means, but I do not remember any details. Unless -- well, I'm not sure, but perhaps an ambulance would have a radio device. Other than that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that you don't know how the units communicated with the command post on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they used couriers. I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know by what means it was communicated that the other two soldiers had been wounded to the command post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think someone came over to tell us that, but I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You said that there was firing throughout the day. You repeated that on several occasions in your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the nearby villages, yes, there was shooting non-stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you recall at what time were those two soldiers wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning, before noon. I don't know at what time exactly, but not after 10.00 I think, say between 8.00 and 10.00. Now you're asking me about things which took place a long time ago. It probably is somewhere in the documents at the health centre. The fact is that they were wounded on that day and that the other soldier was wounded that day; but at what time, I don't know. It would be too much to expect of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand you completely, and I also believe that back in 2002 your recollection was better than today. Can you remember who was at the command post together with you and your commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, maybe we should go to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is P2019, the war diary. Could the witness please be shown page 11.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. [Interpretation] Could we enlarge the B/C/S version. Please focus on the 27th of November [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Witness K90, this is the war diary of your unit where it is stated that two soldiers, volunteers, had been wounded at 8.35. Does this tally with what you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall what time it was. We were soaking wet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go on to the next page in the English. That's the next page, and the date being the 28th of April. The Serbian version should remain. Your Honour, it is the 28th of April, line 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the document, it reads that the other soldier who you mentioned got wounded the next day at 2.35 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Completely incorrect. I can swear before this Tribunal that the soldier you are thinking about now and the other two were wounded the same day. The blockade was not the next day; but, rather, we began with it in the morning at 5.00 and they were wounded the same day. Who wrote this and under what conditions, I don't know; but I know that the three or wounded on the same day. That is 100 percent sure and correct. You (redacted) (redacted) same day. There was no blockade the next day; therefore, no one could have been wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As for whether there was a blockade the next day remains to be established, but I wanted to ask you this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just before I move to the next group of questions, could we please move into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in relation to one of the last answers given by this witness, K90, where he claimed that the blockade took place only on one day, the 27th of April, 1999, I would like to draw your attention to 2019, that is in front of you. The 28th of April is its date, 1999, and it says there at 0220 the Siptars tried to get out of the blockade in the area of Kikes. The group was liquidated, broken up. I cannot see this right. A large quantity of ammunition and mortar -- hand-held mortar shells were seized.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What is your comment? What do you say to this that in the diary it says that the blockade went on --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. If that was on the 27th, the event that I testified about, that's when we set up the blockade. What happened on the next day, we weren't there. I wasn't there. I claim that this man was wounded on the 27th; that is to say -- well, I'm not saying the 27th. I'm saying on the day when this event occurred, when those two were wounded. So I did not say exactly what date it was. I did not say it in my statement either. I wasn't sure what date it was. I know that it was in April, but I did not know which date. So in the statement it also says that I don't know exactly what date it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you give shorter answers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you say that the following day you were not there, was the blockade still there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. We all left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That's fine. That answers the question. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to draw your attention to the date after that, the 29th, where it also says that the blockade was over in the Reka area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. K90, now I am going to ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, can I have a reference to where that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't see on the 29th that it says the blockade is over.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that not the first line of the 29th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, not in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: May I see Serbian version next page. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you mean the earlier page? It must be an earlier page, Mr. Visnjic. We've now got May on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that Mr. Hannis is right, actually. It was my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, bearing in mind the time I have left over, I suggest that for the rest of my cross-examination we go into private session. I have questions where I am going to be referring to names, so quite simply I think it would be more reasonable to deal with it quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you indicated that on that occasion an aerosol can was used to light the homes on fire. I would like to ask you, first of all: Did you bring that aerosol can or someone from your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was that something that was just found in the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Such cans were not -- were not standard issue in your military kits, were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So, sir, the impression that I'm getting is that the events that you described at paragraphs 36 through 37 were all individual events, individual crimes, committed by yourselves and the other persons present, who were all drunk at the time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you say "crimes" here. We didn't kill anyone. The fact is that those two houses were set on fire. There was no one in those houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You did not report what had happened, that the houses had been burned, to either the police SUP or any other police or army authorities, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't my job. We had our superior who was with us, so it wasn't our job. It was our superior whose duty it was, not us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to move on. You have several times stated, yesterday, that there was a -- there was not an active KLA presence in the area during the relevant time-period. I'd like to ask you at paragraph 47 of your statement, you describe the ambush and killing of five policemen. And I want to ask you: Isn't it correct that this ambush and killing was reported to have been carried out by the KLA on a roadway in the region precisely where you said you did not know of any KLA activity. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We misunderstand one another. There were no KLA activities in the town, at least not public activities. In the village where the incident with the policeman occurred, or rather, on the road, we didn't go there because of what I stated previously, that a major of the Territorial Defence guaranteed there would be no problems. Whether they passed through that village or not, they had not done anything to anyone before that; and then they killed those policemen and that was it. Up to that point, there had been no public activities that might indicate their presence, except of course that they continually attacked from the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That area where the attack on the five policemen that you talk about occurred, isn't it correct that that roadway is within the area that was under the blockade -- that later was part of the blockade that you are testifying about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I can't say exactly where the policemen were killed, but it was on that road, on the Djakovica-Junik road, somewhere in the whereabouts of that village, and that's quite clear. There's nothing in dispute about it. I can't tell you exactly where. I can't pin-point the very spot, but it was in that area on that road. That area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I have to turn off my microphone so as not to interfere with your voice distortion device. Sir, I'd like to put something forward to you. We've heard evidence here in this court from another military policeman from the VJ. He was a witness here, Mr. K73, whose unit was engaged in the activities, was in the villages rather than part of the blockade, approaching Korenica on the night of the 27th of April, 1999. And he testified to the fact that there were KLA in the area, and on that night a group of KLA stumbled upon his unit that was based in a village and engaged in a firefight leading to the death of one soldier and the self-inflicted wound of another. This is at transcript page 3332, lines 1 through 20. Sir, two questions for you: First of all, do you have knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I am testifying about the part of the road from the crossroads to the entry to the village. I was on that road that day. What happened on the other side of the village, beyond the village, I don't know because I didn't go there. Whether there were other soldiers there, I don't think our military police was there, but there may have been some military police from another unit that was not part of our unit. So I'm not denying that. What I am saying is that in the area where that incident occurred, there were no other men apart from the ones in our battalion, at least as far as I was able to see. As for the area beyond the village, I had no idea who was there. I don't exclude the possibility they were there, but I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you, therefore, concede that since you were not everywhere, that there could very well have been KLA presence and KLA resistance within the area that was the subject of the blockade and the operation? Would you concede that that is possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we specify a time-period for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would specify the 27th and the 28th of April, when the blockade was in effect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I might be willing to concede what you have just said, provided I knew what area they were in. Because in the area I was in, there was not a single KLA member. Whether there were any on the other side of the village, we couldn't see that. It's possible, but I can say neither yes nor no, because I wasn't there. I didn't even hear about that man being killed or wounded. I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, one of my colleagues, I believe it was Mr. Ackerman, had asked you about the report I believe in the diary, regarding the two soldiers that were wounded during that operation. I believe they were wounded on the evening of the 27th. And you disagreed with the report in the diary. The question I'd like to ask you relates to the wounding of the one other individual, and we have an exhibit offered by the Prosecution called P2569, which perhaps we should not put on the public display insofar as it may identify the witness, given the persons -- the officer who signed it. But, sir, this document signed by your commander talks about the wounding of the one individual which occurred, again according to your commander, on the 28th of April, the second day of the blockade; and this report specifically states that he was accidentally wounded by friendly fire opened by members of the MUP. Would you concede that had the -- had the two men who you claim were wounded by the MUP -- actually, had been wounded by the MUP, why wouldn't it have been reported the same way this one incident was reported, saying it was friendly fire? Why would there be a need to say that the fire came from a group of civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the person you are speaking about is from Republika Srpska. The other two are citizens of Serbia. Maybe this means something. I'm sure that the two who were wounded, the people who brought them there, I spoke to both of them, they said they were wounded by stray bullets. I'm not saying the police shot them, but they were the only ones shooting in that area. There was nobody else who would have fired shots. I didn't see the KLA shooting. I didn't see the army shooting, so it's quite logical. Not for a moment did I think they were aiming at soldiers. I'm just saying that they were wounded by stray bullets. One was simply grazed and the other one was more seriously wounded and he didn't even come back to the unit. I can see the document you're showing me. I can see part of what it says, but I don't know of any other reason, unless I were to engage in speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I posit that what you're doing is engaging in speculation, because you really don't know where the stray bullet came from, do you -- the stray bullet or bullets, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. From the village, from the village in which the policemen were. They had already passed the first houses. So they could only have been wounded from there, because, sir, if we exclude the possibility of civilians shooting, which would be an absurdity, on the left-hand side if you cross the river our units were there, towards the border post, and they were not shooting. The soldiers who were there were not shooting. They had no reason to shoot towards the river where our people were, so only the civilians -- I don't know. It's very difficult to say that the civilians were shooting, people who didn't know where they were. I don't know. I understand your situation, but I cannot affirm for a fact that they were shot by civilians; that's absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So your understanding has to exclude the civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I took those people to Djakovica. I saw what they looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, as I indicated, we have some time constraints and I would, please, appreciate, especially since it causes problems with your voice distortion here, that you confine your answers to my questions and try not to interrupt questions. Now, if we could focus on the NATO bombings. You have testified in response to questions posed by my colleagues that the NATO bombings were quite constant and that they made communications very difficult, indeed impossible. Now, I'd like to focus briefly on the event that you have described in paragraph 46 relating to Korisa village. First of all, that occurred on the 13th of May, 1999. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Does the information that you have tell you at least that it occurred at approximately midnight or just before midnight on whatever day it occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I learned this from my conversations with people who were there on the spot and in my conversation with the investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what date it was, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, so you learned some of this from the investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No. I learned this after the war in Kosovo three, four, five months later in my conversations with the policemen who were there on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I suppose these sources that advised you of this event did not tell you that among the wounded from this event were two policemen, Dejan Nikolic and Ivan Djordjevic, both of the Prizren SUP. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. Today, at the beginning of the session, I said it was the person at the petrol station who was there, who told me that they thought they had all been killed. That's how strong the explosions were. They thought everything had toppled down when the explosion went off, and I wrote that. I didn't say categorically that that's how it was -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can move on to another topic. Now, yesterday, you talked about the -- about the matters contained in paragraph 47 of your statement, the arrival of police and Frenki's to Djakovica. Now, you've today somewhat, I believe, changed your description of these Frenki's and what occurred. Now, first of all, I want to ask you: Is it your testimony that the so-called hats, the familiar hats, that you were describing are, in fact, berets, red berets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, a little hat and a beret are not the same thing. Those two men I saw there with masks on their faces wore little hats, because people changed uniforms very often in our parts. It would depend on a lot of things. Uniforms changed very frequently, and I knew that in some situations even the SAJ wore such hats. Someone from the PJP could also have had such a hat, but it was not part of the standard uniform of the PJP. I did not see the whole unit or the commander of that unit. I saw only those two men, neither more nor less. But I do know --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, I think you will appreciate my concern and need to clarify things because the statement that you have says: "They all wore the familiar Frenki hats," which I take to mean "sesir." Now, yesterday, you testified they wore the red berets, "crvene beretke." There lies my confusion, sir. And you have to understand that and appreciate you are using different terminology to describe these things, and I'm trying to find out what the truth of the matter is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I talked about red berets yesterday, when His Honour asked me who the Frenki's were, I said they were units for special operations. I didn't say the whole unit was there and that those 400 men who all arrived were all Red Berets. I said they were mainly members of the PJP. I saw those two with the little hats and the masks on their faces, and I thought it was the unit for special operations. I had no reason to ask them whether they were that unit, but that's what I thought. I may have been wrong. But judging by the equipment they had, I thought they were from that unit. Now, whether the whole unit was there or not, I can't say because I didn't see them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that you may be wrong, but I would like to ask you this: Those two individuals that you saw, they came in a private automobile. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Yes, in a private car, yes. In a civilian vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I believe today -- well strike that. As far as the buses are concerned, did all these buses that you describe come at the same time, in one convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I don't think so. They came individually. No, no, no way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Where exactly did you see these buses and vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would come to Djakovica, to the town for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What part of town, for instance, and where were you situated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Near the church in the area where the bombs didn't fall; not near the SUP in Djakovica but nearer the river, nearer that village. So we saw those buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was anyone else with you at the time who could vouch for your story?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people working at the check-point, the policemen and the soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you see each of these buses and vehicles with the PJP yourself, with your own eyes, or are we hearing what you heard from other people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the members of the PJP passed by me. They couldn't go anywhere else, and some even went there by bus and then the bus came back. How far it took them, I don't know, but I know I did see buses, as I had says here about ten. It could have been more or less, but around ten. I did see buses. I saw them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, as far as the PJP are concerned, you stated that you had never seen the insignia of the PJP in Kosovo and, in fact, couldn't identify any emblems of the police. How could you be certain that these persons were PJP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wore camouflage uniforms with those trousers and those jackets, not green but kind of yellowish. And, secondly, when the policemen were withdrawing, the buses came to pick them up. The same buses that had taken them there took them back from there. When the area was clear, they came to pick them up. There's no doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, did they have "PJP" written on the side of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what's the relevance to the answer that the same buses came back to collect them? We're trying to work out how you recognised these people as PJP. And unless the bus said "PJP," the bus has got nothing to do with identifying them. So how did you recognise that they were PJP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By the uniforms, by the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me one other thing. When you told me yesterday that there were people with red berets, who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You asked me how one could recognise Frenki's men, and I said they were the Red Berets. They did not wear red berets in the war, not in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At least --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the nature of the hats that the two men were wearing that you referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hats. They were hats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was their distinctive feature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Normal hats worn to one side. These same people came to look for that colleague of mine to get them to go back to that unit, not those two but others. And there was no doubt that this was a unit for special operations because they came to get him. Now, whether those two were members or not, that's a different story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have described them as wearing the familiar Frenki hats. Now, tell me what is distinctive about a Frenki hat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hats, yes. Well, masks and hats. No special characteristics or maybe I don't recall. You can't really inspect each individual uniform in such a situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So how is it you know that they are Frenki's men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, they might have been Frenki's men judging by the hats. I allowed for the possibility that someone else could have had such hats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what I would like to know is what do these hats look like that enable you to decide that they're Frenki's men? Tell me what they look like, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, the problem is that they came in a civilian vehicle --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just tell me what the hats looked like, please. Never mind the vehicle. Tell me about the hats.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were camouflage hats, no special characteristic. I can't even remember what they looked like now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we've exhausted that area, and we'll move on to another one. Now, at paragraphs 43 and 44, you stated that your unit and your unit alone was involved in the relocation of the civilians from many villages and hamlets around Djakovica in mid-April. Was it just -- when you say your unit, are we just talking about the eight of you set forth in paragraph 30, including the two volunteers who were not from -- or who were from another country -- from another ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could focus on the blockade. You have described the command post where you were with your commander. How far was this command post from the centre of the village of Korenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I did not enter the village, not farther away from the first houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: From the position of the command post, could you see very clearly the houses in Korenica village; that is, the village itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The beginning of the village, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You stated that you had not been in Korenica. Were you personally in any of the other surrounding villages on the 27th of April, 1999, during the blockade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When those two soldiers were wounded and when the commander ordered me to go by the river and to get those men out, I wrote that down in my statement as the village of Meja. That's what I think today as well. To this day I think that it's the village of Meja. Maybe I made a mistake, but I think that that is the village of Meja. It doesn't change the situation in terms of what happened. I went to the village and I got those people out from near the river. Maybe I just made a mistake in terms of the name of the village, but not in terms of what it was that had happened. I went to get them for sure, and there was this other soldier from Sombor who went. I don't know his name. And the man who was asking me a few moments ago, he didn't ask me about him. He did not mention his name. The man is from Sombor, and he's an active soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can we be certain, though, that the village you went to was below or south of Korenica, not above Korenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Parallel with the road it was, but the left of the river. So, say we're moving from Djakovica towards Junik, then it's on the left. The village starts with a big mill and then houses go on by the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, again, coming from Djakovica, Korenica would be on the right. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards Junik, when you go towards Junik, then on the right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, you testified that police were shooting randomly into homes. Could you see that happening in Meja and Korenica from your position at the VJ command post? Did you personally see this or is this something that you assumed or heard about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it started, when they started entering the village, then I saw what was going on in the village because I really did not go into the village itself, but I saw at the beginning of the village when the first houses were involved, when they started shooting at the houses first and then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, correct me if I'm wrong, sir, but the infantry forces in the village, whatever their make-up was, they were advancing towards the front of the village, towards your position. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, from our positions towards the centre of the village. Now, were there other units on the other side, I don't know, but it was from us into the other direction. As we were here this way, this is where the road is, we were here roughly, and then they moved off from us into the village. There were other units, too, or rather, I don't know whether there were other units on the other side because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that the infantry forces were attempting to move people away from the check-point at the Meja Orize-Djakovica crossroad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about a point that was on the bridge into the entrance of Brekovac; whereas, I am talking about the spot where policemen were. This is a small crossroads between the dirt road and the road for cars. So we're not talking about the same spot.
